title: Ecclesiastes 2:12–26
context: The Preacher weighs wisdom against madness and folly. Wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness, yet the same fate, death, comes to wise and fool alike, and both are forgotten. He comes to hate life and his labor, since he must leave it to a successor who may be wise or foolish, and he gives his heart up to despair. Yet the chapter ends by commending eating, drinking, and finding enjoyment in labor as coming from the hand of God, who gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to the one who pleases him. Both traditions read this close as gift and not as license, and many read it alongside the book’s conclusion in Ecclesiastes 12:13–14. In 2:25, the Hebrew as rendered by WEB has the speaker say no one can eat or enjoy more than he; some translations follow a reading that refers to God instead, and the sense is debated.

verses.text: I turned myself to consider wisdom, madness, and folly; for what can the king’s successor do? Just that which has been done long ago.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher turns to consider wisdom, madness, and folly, asking what the king’s successor can do. Arminian readers note that the question suggests no one after him will discover more than he did.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse is difficult and has been read in more than one way, and they hold its sense loosely. Shared ground: both traditions read it as introducing a comparison between wisdom and folly.

verses.text: Then I saw that wisdom excels folly, as far as light excels darkness.
verses.arminianNotes: He sees that wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness. Arminian readers note that despite all his doubts, the Preacher affirms the real value of wisdom for living.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comparison as consistent with the wisdom tradition of Proverbs. Both traditions read the verse as a firm affirmation that keeps the book from simple despair about wisdom.

verses.text: The wise man’s eyes are in his head, and the fool walks in darkness—and yet I perceived that one event happens to them all.
verses.arminianNotes: The wise man’s eyes are in his head while the fool walks in darkness, yet one event happens to all. Arminian readers note the tension between wisdom’s advantage and the shared fate of death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the “one event” as death, which comes to wise and foolish alike. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as holding together wisdom’s value and its limits, without resolving the tension.

verses.text: Then I said in my heart, “As it happens to the fool, so will it happen even to me; and why was I then more wise?” Then I said in my heart that this also is vanity.
verses.arminianNotes: He reasons that the fool’s fate will also be his, and asks why he became wise. Arminian readers see personal honesty about the troubling question of what wisdom gains in the face of death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear a searching question that the book takes seriously and only partly answers. Shared ground: the closing verdict of vanity is candid, and neither tradition takes it as a final rejection of wisdom.

verses.text: For of the wise man, even as of the fool, there is no memory forever, since in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. Indeed, the wise man must die just like the fool!
verses.arminianNotes: The wise, like the fool, are not remembered forever, and the wise man dies just like the fool. Arminian readers note the link with 1:11, where forgetting falls on every generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as placing all human distinction under the shadow of death. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an observation under the sun, which many read alongside Ecclesiastes 12:13–14.

verses.text: So I hated life, because the work that is worked under the sun was grievous to me; for all is vanity and a chasing after wind.
verses.arminianNotes: He hated life, for the work done under the sun grieved him. Arminian readers note that the Preacher records a real emotional low, and Scripture does not hide such moments of despair.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the honesty of the verse as part of the book’s value for readers facing similar feelings. Both traditions read it as a stage in the Preacher’s reflection, not his final word.

verses.text: I hated all my labor in which I labored under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.
verses.arminianNotes: He hated his labor because he must leave it to the one who comes after him. Arminian readers see the frustration of investing a lifetime of work that will pass to another’s control.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as showing that no one can secure the fruit of their labor forever. Shared ground: both traditions read the complaint as an honest reflection on the limits of human control.

verses.text: Who knows whether he will be a wise man or a fool? Yet he will have rule over all of my labor in which I have labored, and in which I have shown myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity.
verses.arminianNotes: No one knows if the successor will be wise or foolish, yet he will rule over all the Preacher’s work. Arminian readers note the uncertainty about what others will do with what we leave behind.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as one more reason to hold achievements loosely. Both traditions read the closing judgment that this also is vanity as the Preacher’s response to that uncertainty.

verses.text: Therefore I began to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labor in which I had labored under the sun.
verses.arminianNotes: He began to give his heart up to despair over all his labor. Arminian readers note the depth of the Preacher’s discouragement, which the book reports frankly rather than smoothing over.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the despair as the natural outcome of viewing labor only under the sun. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a low point that the end of the chapter answers in part with 2:24–26.

verses.text: For there is a man whose labor is with wisdom, with knowledge, and with skillfulness; yet he shall leave it for his portion to a man who has not labored for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.
verses.arminianNotes: A man may labor with wisdom and skill, yet leave his portion to one who did not labor for it. Arminian readers see the apparent unfairness of inheritance, which the Preacher calls a great evil.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as illustrating the frustrations of life in a world marked by death. Both traditions read the complaint as honest observation, not as a rule against leaving an inheritance.

verses.text: For what does a man have of all his labor and of the striving of his heart, in which he labors under the sun?
verses.arminianNotes: What does a man have from all his labor and striving under the sun? Arminian readers note that the question returns to 1:3, framing the whole section with the issue of lasting gain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as underlining that labor alone cannot provide ultimate meaning. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as rhetorical, inviting reflection rather than expecting a simple answer.

verses.text: For all his days are sorrows, and his travail is grief; yes, even in the night his heart takes no rest. This also is vanity.
verses.arminianNotes: His days are sorrow, his toil is grief, and even at night his heart finds no rest. Arminian readers note the vivid picture of anxiety that follows a person into the hours meant for sleep.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as describing the restlessness of labor pursued without contentment. Both traditions read it as an honest portrait of toil, setting up the contrast with the enjoyment commended in 2:24.

verses.text: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
verses.arminianNotes: Nothing is better than to eat, drink, and find enjoyment in labor, and this is from the hand of God. Arminian readers see the simple joys of life received as God’s gift, not as a license for indulgence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as pointing beyond human effort to God as the giver of enjoyment. Shared ground: both traditions read 2:24–26 as commending grateful contentment, a theme the book returns to more than once.

verses.text: For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher asks who can eat or enjoy more than he. Arminian readers note that the WEB follows a reading in which the Preacher speaks of himself, stressing that he has tested pleasure to its limit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that some translations follow a reading that refers to God rather than the speaker, and the sense is debated. Both traditions read the verse as supporting 2:24, that enjoyment is from God’s hand.

verses.text: For to the man who pleases him, God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he gives travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him who pleases God. This also is vanity and a chasing after wind.
verses.arminianNotes: God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to the one who pleases him, while the sinner receives toil. Arminian readers see God’s gifts as fitting those who walk in his ways; on gift and seeking, see the existing box at Proverbs 2:6.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign giving as the source of every good the righteous enjoy. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as affirming God as giver, and the existing Proverbs 2:6 box already sets out their differences, so none is added here.
